title: Humor
hook: Zen laughter, Ryokan's games, Ikkyu's jokes
tomorrow: why did an old monk turn down the Buddha's offer of an easier life?

segments.voice: Yesterday, glad for them: the Buddha's double cry for Kondañña, and sādhu said for someone else. Mai said hers for Khoa's chant, sting and all.

A phone goes off in the middle of a silent exam, and the whole room cracks up. Laughter loves the exact moment it isn't supposed to happen. Zen keeps stories like that. Here's one people tell about Ikkyu, a Japanese Zen monk remembered for his poems and his jokes. As a boy, he broke his teacher's prized teacup. He heard the teacher coming, hid the pieces behind his back, and asked: why do people have to die? Everything dies when its time comes, the teacher said. Ikkyu held out the pieces. It was your teacup's time.
screen: `LAUGHTER AT THE WORST MOMENT.` → `IKKYU, A BROKEN CUP.` → `WHY DO PEOPLE DIE?` → `IT WAS YOUR TEACUP'S TIME.`

segments.voice: So can something holy be funny? Zen's answer is the joke itself. The boy didn't dodge the teaching; he handed it back, in pieces. Whatever comes together comes apart. In the Long Discourses, the Buddha's last words to his monks begin there: all conditioned things pass away. Seeing that clearly loosens the grip, and in Buddhist teaching the grip, craving and clinging, is where suffering starts. What do we grip hardest? Ourselves: our dignity, our image, the version of us that never drops anything. A good laugh can pry those fingers open. Zen lore keeps stories of laughing monks. Ikkyu's jokes. Ryokan, who, in a story people tell, hid so well in a children's game that he was still hiding the next morning. Budai, the laughing monk with the big belly and the sack. Their lightness isn't careless. It's not holding on. A neighbor tradition says something close. Proverbs, in the King James Bible: "A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones." Both see a light heart as good for a person. The honest difference: Proverbs sets that merry heart inside a life lived before God, as part of wisdom. The Zen joke points somewhere else: at how little there is to cling to, even in yourself.
screen: `WHATEVER COMES TOGETHER COMES APART.` · `CLINGING, EVEN TO DIGNITY.` · `IKKYU, RYOKAN, BUDAI.` · `A MERRY HEART, IN PROVERBS.` · then, large: `LIGHTLY.`

segments.voice: Sit as you are and let three things soften: the shoulders, the jaw, the corners of the mouth. If a smile wants to come, let it; if not, that's fine too. Then rest with the breath, and hold this moment the way you'd hold a teacup you know won't last forever: carefully, and lightly.
Humor: in Zen, a laugh that loosens the grip. Ikkyu's broken teacup, handed back as a teaching.
The line for today: lightly, the way Ikkyu held out the pieces of the cup. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1763 COUNTS.` → `A LIFE OF PRACTICE · 38 OF 45.` → `TOMORROW: WHY DID AN OLD MONK TURN DOWN THE BUDDHA'S OFFER OF AN EASIER LIFE?`

howItsDone: Zen communities keep funny stories of their teachers and tell them as teachings; the Buddha's teaching on impermanence, that all conditioned things pass away, is recited and reflected on in Buddhist practice.

chat.says: dropped the bell in the big silence. CLANG. ava was visiting and laughed hardest. should i be mortified?
options: laugh with her. like Ikkyu's cup, things fall and pass. hold your dignity lightly.
laugh it off, sure, but Zen humor is just a break from the real practice.
act like it was on purpose. a good leader never looks like she slipped.
chat.meaning: Ikkyu handed back a broken cup as a teaching: everything passes. Zen humor loosens our grip on things, and on our own image.

tie.story: Ikkyu broke his teacher's teacup, then reminded him that everything dies when its time comes.
tie.friend: Mai can laugh with Ava at the clang: the silence, and her dignity, were never hers to keep.

Ikkyu.meaning: a Japanese Zen monk remembered for his poems and jokes

Ryokan.meaning: a Japanese Zen monk and poet who played with village children

Budai.meaning: a laughing monk of Chinese legend, with a big belly and sack

Zen.meaning: a Buddhist school, Chan in China and Zen in Japan, centered on meditation

Long Discourses.meaning: the Digha Nikaya, a collection of the Buddha's longer talks

notes: Shape: wisdom (one question: can something holy be funny?). Unity thread: Proverbs 17:22 (KJV) as the neighbor's words; shared: a light heart is good for a person; honest difference: Proverbs sets it in a life before God, the Zen joke points at non-clinging. No ranking. Mai's storyline: her best friend Ava visits the chùa (the monthly meeting with the best friend's world); Mai drops the bell during the silence and Ava laughs hardest.
Ikkyu's teacup: a widely retold Zen anecdote, voiced as 'one people tell'; no canonical source. Confirm it is fair to attach to Ikkyu.
Ryokan hiding through the night in a children's game: anecdote voiced as 'a story people tell'. Day 1600 used Ryokan's temari games; this day uses a different story. Confirm.
Budai: the laughing monk of Chinese legend, linked in later tradition with Maitreya; described only by his image. Confirm.

DN 16: the Buddha's last words, that conditioned things are subject to passing away, with an urging to strive on with heedfulness; voiced as 'begin there: all conditioned things pass away'. Paraphrased; confirm.
Proverbs 17:22 quoted from the KJV; confirm wording.
Surprising fact: the teacup story turns the teaching on impermanence into a confession.
